title: Transforming search and discovery using LLMs — Tejaswi & Vinesh, Instacart

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk is primarily about using LLMs to improve search and discovery at Instacart, covering query understanding, query rewrites, discovery content generation, and ranking. The content centers on large-scale product search and discovery for an e-commerce grocery platform. The described LLM-based search components are deployed in production with reported A/B test results and serving infrastructure. Requires familiarity with search architecture and ML concepts but remains accessible to practitioners. Recorded conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair. Provides concrete quantitative metrics, production A/B test results, and specific query examples.

summary: Vinesh and Tejaswi from Instacart's search and discovery ML team discuss using LLMs to address limitations of conventional search engines in grocery e-commerce. Grocery search must simultaneously support quick restocking purchases and new product discovery, the latter being valuable for advertisers and basket size growth. Traditional search faces challenges with overly broad queries (cold-start), highly specific long-tail queries (insufficient engagement data), and difficulty discovering related products. The team focused on upleveling query understanding, the most upstream part of the search stack. For query-to-category classification, providing top K converting categories as LLM context yielded tail-query precision gains of 18 percentage points and recall gains of 70 percentage points. For query rewrites, LLMs generated substitute, broad, and synonymous rewrites, reducing zero-result queries significantly. A unified LLM also resolved cascading errors, such as a 'hmm' query correctly identified as a kombucha brand but misspelled by a traditional spell corrector as 'hummus.' Beyond query understanding, the team used LLMs to generate discovery-oriented content on search results pages—substitute items (e.g., swordfish → tilapia) and complementary items (e.g., sushi → Asian cooking ingredients, Japanese drinks). An initial basic generation prompt produced common-sense answers that users didn't engage with (e.g., 'protein' returned chicken/tofu rather than protein bars/shakes). Augmenting prompts with Instacart domain knowledge—top converting categories, query understanding annotations, and subsequent user queries—significantly improved both engagement and revenue. For serving, Instacart pre-computes LLM outputs for historical search logs in batch mode and serves from a feature store for low latency. Three key challenges emerged: aligning generation with business metrics like revenue, ranking (traditional PCTR/PCBR models failed, requiring diversity-based ranking), and evaluation (hallucination detection and product adherence, addressed using LLM-as-judge). The team also discussed Ask Instacart, which handles natural language queries by mapping them to search intents, reinforcing the importance of injecting platform context and robust automated evaluation. Overall takeaways: LLM world knowledge helps tail queries, combining domain knowledge with LLMs drives topline wins, and evaluation is harder than anticipated.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Importance of Search in Grocery E-commerce
sections.summary: Speakers introduce themselves as part of Instacart's search and discovery ML team. They explain that grocery search has a dual role: enabling quick restocking purchases and new product discovery. New discovery benefits customers, advertisers, and the platform through larger basket sizes.

sections.title: Challenges with Conventional Search Engines
sections.summary: Two classes of challenging queries are identified: overly broad queries (e.g., 'snacks') with too many matching products and cold-start issues, and highly specific queries (e.g., 'unsweetened plant-based yogurt') with insufficient engagement data. Customers also report difficulty discovering related products, unlike browsing physical grocery store aisles.

sections.title: LLM-Based Query-to-Category Classification
sections.summary: The team improved query-to-category classification using LLMs. Initial attempts without user behavior context failed online A/B tests. Providing top K converting categories as context solved the mismatch, yielding 18-point precision and 70-point recall improvements for tail queries. Example: 'Wner soda' correctly identified as ginger ale brand.

sections.title: LLM-Based Query Rewrites
sections.summary: Query rewrites help handle varying retailer catalog sizes. LLMs generate substitute, broad, and synonymous rewrites (e.g., avocado oil → olive oil / healthy cooking oil / avocado extract). Upgrading to better LLM models improved offline evaluation, and online tests showed a large drop in zero-result queries.

sections.title: Scoring, Serving, and Future Directions
sections.summary: Instacart pre-computes LLM outputs for head/torso queries offline and serves from cache for low latency, falling back to existing models for long tail with plans to replace them with a distilled Llama model. The team suggests consolidating multiple query understanding models into a single SLM/LLM for consistency. A 'hmm' query example is introduced.

sections.title: Unified Model Benefits and Discovery Content Generation
sections.summary: The 'hmm' query was correctly identified by LLM as a kombucha brand, but a traditional spell corrector changed it to 'hummus,' confusing users. A unified LLM resolved this. The team then introduces LLM-generated discovery content on search results pages: substitute items (e.g., swordfish → tilapia) and complementary items (e.g., sushi → Asian cooking ingredients, Japanese drinks), improving engagement and revenue per search.

sections.title: Prompt Augmentation with Instacart Domain Knowledge
sections.summary: A basic generation prompt for complementary and substitute items looked good offline but users didn't engage because LLM gave common-sense answers (protein → chicken/tofu, not protein bars/shakes). Augmenting prompts with top converting categories, query understanding annotations, and subsequent user queries dramatically improved engagement and revenue.

sections.title: Serving Discovery Content and Key Challenges
sections.summary: Discovery content is served via offline batch processing of historical search logs stored in a feature store. Three challenges emerged: aligning generation with revenue metrics, ranking (traditional PCTR/PCBR failed, requiring diversity-based ranking), and evaluation (hallucination detection and product adherence using LLM-as-judge).

sections.title: Summary Takeaways and Q&A
sections.summary: Key takeaways: LLM world knowledge improved tail-query understanding; combining domain knowledge with LLMs drove topline wins; evaluation was harder than anticipated. Q&A covers Ask Instacart for natural language queries, emphasizing the need to inject Instacart context, build robust automated evaluation, and pass downstream context (e.g., Mother's Day → women's perfumes, not generic perfumes).

demonstrations: Prompt design for query-to-category classification using top converting categories as context
Query rewrite types: substitute (avocado oil → olive oil), broad (→ healthy cooking oil), synonymous (→ avocado extract)
Example of LLM behavioral mismatch: 'protein' query mapped to chicken/tofu instead of protein shakes/bars
Example of improved precision: 'Wner soda' correctly identified as ginger ale brand
Discovery content examples: swordfish → seafood alternatives like tilapia; sushi → Asian cooking ingredients and Japanese drinks
Domain alignment examples: 'dishes' = cookware not food; 'Thanksgiving dishes' = food not cookware
Ask Instacart: natural language query 'healthy foods for a three-year-old' mapped to fruit slices and similar items
Mother's Day context example: passing 'women's perfumes' context downstream rather than generic 'perfumes'
limitations: Initial LLM approach without user behavior context produced poor online A/B test results
BERT-based models showed limited improvement relative to increased latency
Traditional models have low coverage for tail queries due to engagement data sparsity
Offline pre-computation only covers head and torso queries; long tail still requires fallback models
Basic LLM generation prompts produced common-sense answers that users did not engage with
Traditional PCTR/PCBR ranking models did not work for discovery content, requiring diversity-based ranking
Evaluating LLM-generated content for hallucinations and product adherence was harder than anticipated
Injecting sufficient Instacart context into natural language query models is essential for decent results
